b: “All eyes will be on you.” It’s a warning that Marie Antoinette can’t yet fathom, because she is, after all, only a child when she’s forced to leave her friends, a cute little pug, and all of Austria behind to enter the court of Louis XV. Greeted outside the gates of Versailles by the Comtesse de Noailles (Judy Davis), Marie Antoinette (Kirsten Dunst) hugs the woman, whose mortification is most visible in her severe neckline. This young girl will need molding, and implicit in her cold reception is the difficulty of her pilgrim’s progress toward queenhood. It’s a funeral procession into a gilded confine where she’ll be fashioned into something she’s decidedly not, and where her every movement will be so closely monitored that the clothes on her back become not unlike mood rings, absorbing the colors of her traumatized essence. The film’s last shot is telling: A beautiful, bejeweled bird, this girl will be ripped from her cage, leaving only feathers and loads of crap behind.

Does empathy explain why Sofia Coppola chose the story of Marie Antoinette as the follow-up to her hugely successful Lost in Translation? No other royal in history was so brutally and unforgivably held up for scrutiny, and no other female filmmaker has had her talent, privilege, and success so insensitively begrudged by critics, male and female alike. The prissy disdain for Coppola’s films in some circles could be described as an act of sexual terrorism, but Marie Antoinette is scarcely defensive, which isn’t to say that it’s without meaning or that its commentary on its titular queen’s rise and fall isn’t barbed.

Back in 2006, I was guilty of holding the soundtrack against Marie Antoinette, sight unseen, but the film itself quickly made me see the light, and it was as lucid as the rising sun that Marie Antoinette takes in after a long birthday celebration, on a dawn noisy with friendly chatter and the clink of champagne glasses. The collection of mostly new wave and post-punk anthems, like the thoroughly modern performances Coppola doesn’t have to coax very hard out of her actors (only Marie Antoinette’s young daughter speaks French in the film), serves as a great, often funny distancing effect—an attempt to chart the space between us and the past, but also to bring us closer to the truth. Smart and playful, the songs illuminate the intricacies of a discouraged woman’s state of mind, from the horror of her initiation into a foreign world (Aphex Twin’s “Jynweythek Ylow”) to her thirst for material possessions (Bow Wow Wow’s “I Want Candy”).

Marie Antoinette compares favorably to The New World and, even more so, to The Lost City—two tales of Edens stripped of their fruit. Andy Garcia’s ode to his bygone Cuba had no room in its imagination for the country’s impoverished masses, because Garcia only understood what was taken away from his family. Coppola’s vision is less pathological: The poor (and their means of execution) don’t figure into her film because Marie Antoinette, like her equally juvenile king, Louis XVI (Jason Schwartzman), had no concept of proletarian existence, holed up as they were inside their palace, far from France’s starving, restless populace. Their heartache is of a different sort: the horror of having their private lives on constant display before a snippy, prying court, which prominently includes Molly Shannon and Shirley Henderson as Louis’s very funny, gossipy aunts and Asia Argento as the very cruel Madame du Barry, the cat to Dunst’s canary.

Coppola is obsessed with Marie Antoinette’s pleasure, contriving for her a series of mini revolutions (she claps, to everyone’s shock, after an opera performance and, later, carries on an affair with a dashing Swedish count, played by Jamie Dornan) that hint at the girl’s desire to push back against what was preordained—to carve out her own space away from the busy hands of oppression. Cynics may reduce these moments to feminist fiddling, but they’re in fact very humane considerations of the corset-like effect that ritual had on Marie Antoinette’s will.

The film is a great fashion show, but it’s also a great makeover—an elegy to frustration, where every color and sound evokes the longing and rapture of a girl who didn’t understand her adult responsibilities. “Am I here?” she asks while playing a parlor guessing game. Her answer comes later, when she bows to the barbarians at her gates, a gesture that registers as “I am here.” Remarkably, Coppola doesn’t ask us to take Marie Antoinette as she saw herself, but as she probably was: a little girl who didn’t know better.

The Criterion Collection’s 4K UHD presents a new 4K digital restoration, supervised and approved by director Sofia Coppola and director of photography Lance Acord, and the difference from the soft, underwhelming high-def presentations the film has been saddled with until now is striking. Presented in Dolby Vision HDR, Marie Antoinette’s candy-colored palette is rich, but the image never looks synthetic, thanks to a pleasantly film-like grain structure that’s been carefully preserved. Fine detail is vastly improved, from the lace and embroidery of the costumes to the ornate surfaces of Versailles, while the HDR grade lends a soft luminosity to the naturally lit interiors and the sun-dappled grounds of the Petit Trianon.

The 5.1 surround DTS-HD Master Audio track is just as strong. Dialogue is clean and crisp, and ambient effects are spread subtly but effectively across the surround channels, while the film’s lush blend of new wave, post-punk, and baroque music explodes out of the speakers.

Most of the extras are new to this release, starting with an interview with Sofia Coppola, who looks back on the film two decades after its divisive release, and a selected-scene commentary featuring Kirsten Dunst. More illuminating is a program featuring interviews with Lance Acord, production designer KK Barrett, and costume designer Milena Canonero, which digs into the craftsmanship behind the film’s confectionary splendor. Carried over from Sony’s old DVD are the deleted scenes, the trailer, and Jason Schwartzman’s parody short, a tour of the film’s set as Louis XVI told in the shrill style of MTV’s Cribs. Also included is the music video for Phoenix’s “Run Run Run,” while the package is rounded out by an essay by critic Claire Marie Healy.
Two decades on, Sofia Coppola’s still-misunderstood portrait of a girl in a gilded cage finally gets the lavish home-video treatment it deserves. Let the critics eat cake.
